transcript:
This message is from Synchrony Bank who wants to remind you to stay flexible.
Not the 10,000 steps before breakfast, yoga-bending, circus-performing, wish I hadn't done that kind of flexible.
It's about staying financially flexible, like with their high-yield savings account.
You'll earn a great rate without monthly fees or minimums that can slow your progress.
Go to Synchrony.com/NPR. Member FDIC.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
The U.S. economy picked up speed over the summer and grew faster than it did during the spring.
But prices are also rising fast.
NPR's Stephen Besaha reports the new data came from the last major read that voters will get on the economy ahead of the midterm election.
Gross domestic product for the U.S. grew at an annual rate of 3.4 percent, according to a new report out today from the Commerce Department.
That's for July, August and September, and faster than the 2.2 percent growth from the spring.
One reason for the growth is the major investment in artificial intelligence by tech companies.
All the construction and jobs needed to build data centers boosted the economy.
But the Federal Reserve's preferred measure of inflation released today showed prices in September were 3.6 percent higher than a year ago.
Those prices are top of mind for voters as they head to the polls for the midterm elections next week.
Stephen Besaha, NPR News.
Alaska's governor is now ordering an investigation after New York Times report that the campaign of Democratic Senate candidate Mary Pultola
played a part in urging Dan J. Sullivan to run, potentially, as a spoiler considering the fact that the incumbent Republican senator is also named Dan Sullivan.
President Trump, speaking before boarding Air Force One on a campaign trip to South Carolina today, said he considered it fraud and that it will confuse Alaskans trying to vote.
When you look at that, nobody knows what to press. We've done studies. Nobody knows. They have no idea who the Dan Sullivan is.
Alaska public media correspondent Liz Ruskin says promoting spoiler candidates is legal and common in Alaska.
Super PACs on the right and the left poured millions into elevating political unknowns this summer for our primary.
This one's a little different because it involved recruiting a candidate to act as a spoiler that usually doesn't happen in plain view.
That's Liz Ruskin on NPR's Here and Now.
The winter's forecast is out.
National weather agencies say a super El Nino is changing weather patterns around the globe.
Here's NPR's Ava Berger.
We are in for a warmer and wetter winter.
You can think El Nino. It's a natural climate pattern that happens every few years.
Josh Willis is a climate scientist at NASA.
It rises up out of the ocean like Godzilla, and it breathes fire on Indonesia and Southeast Asia.
They're having severe drought and major wildfires, and its tail is kicking up hurricanes and storms and high tides on our end of the Pacific.
Norieasters tend to have a higher chance of walloping the East Coast. The West Coast already has higher sea levels, and the Southwest could get some drought relief.
Ava Berger, NPR News.
U.S. stocks are trading lower this hour. The NASDAQ is now down nearly one and a half percent. It's NPR News.
Defense Secretary Pete Hekseth has asked another top general from the Pentagon, according to at least three U.S. officials not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.
He tells NPR that Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia was a subject of a leak investigation.
Sylvia was head of strategy plans and policy on the Joint Chiefs of Staff.
Sylvia would not have had a direct role in the war with Iran, but it still reflects a highly unusual amount of disruption at senior military levels.
When a college shuts down, students can often qualify to get their student loans forgiven.
But a new lawsuit claims the U.S. Department of Education is not following all the rules of that program. Here's NPR's Corey Turner.
The suit is over what's known as a closed school discharge, which forgives the debts of borrowers who were enrolled at a college when it closed or no more than six months before it closed.
That window of eligibility was expanded by the Biden administration to include more students at several specific schools.
But this new lawsuit argues the Trump administration is quietly ignoring that expansion and rejecting eligible borrowers.
The suit was filed by Student Defense, a nonprofit borrower advocacy group.
The Education Department tells NPR the Biden expansion was both inappropriate and unlawful, but the suit argues federal agency cannot ignore a previous policy without publicly and legally justifying its actions.
Corey Turner, NPR News.
Boards get jet-lagged, too. Journal Science published a study today finding the seaboard known as the Mag Shearwater is common in the British Isles, and it becomes a bit disoriented.
